    <title>MLExpert: Towards a Generalist Agentic Model for Autonomous Machine Learning Engineering</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:56:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22344v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22344v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) are expanding from assisting scientific research and engineering to autonomously developing and improving AI systems, advancing AI for AI (AI4AI) as a pathway toward recursive self-improvement (RSI). Workflow-driven machine learning engineering (MLE) systems provide a practical path toward this pursuit through complex orchestration that manages long-horizon experimentation, while recent MLE systems adopt model-directed interaction, allowing models to autonomously organize experiments and adapt optimization strategies based on execution feedback. However, feedback from each experiment reflects several preceding decisions, and a long MLE run contains many such costly experiments. Training must therefore select useful supervision from long interaction trajectories and learn from intermediate outcomes. We propose a post-training method for autonomous long-horizon MLE optimization and apply it to train MLExpert, a 35B Mixture-of-Experts agentic model. We design the Kaggle-MLE Factory to construct executable tasks and an interaction harness for model-directed experimentation. Hierarchical agentic SFT transfers general tool-use and coding capabilities to MLE through outcome-guided supervision. Windowed Interaction RL (WIRL) treats the multi-turn decisions between successive experiment results as an execution window and assigns it a shared outcome-based reward. Asynchronous collection and policy correction support policy updates before the trajectory ends. On MLE-Bench Lite, MLExpert improves the average medal rate of the base model from 37.9% to 72.7%, achieving performance comparable to larger frontier models such as Kimi-K3 and GLM-5.3. Further experiments show that MLExpert improves performance on NatureBench Lite, agent scaffold optimization, and algorithm optimization, suggesting that the learned optimization capability generalizes to other tasks.</summary>

    <title>GeoState: Learning View-Decoupled Geometry States for 3D World Modeling</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:56:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22343v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Recent 3D world models increasingly use features from geometry foundation models (GFMs) as predictive world states, benefiting from their rich geometric priors. However, the view dependence of these features entangles scene dynamics with camera-induced variation, making the resulting state evolution harder to predict. We propose GeoState, a view-decoupled geometry representation for predictive 3D world modeling that separates scene-state evolution from camera-dependent observation. Specifically, a scene tokenizer aggregates multi-view GFM features into a view-decoupled scene state, which a geometry decoder queries using camera rays. An autoregressive world model then predicts future scene states, while camera motion is modeled separately. The predicted states can therefore be decoded under either predicted or externally specified cameras, while retaining a single context-derived scale throughout the rollout without per-frame scale alignment. Experiments show that GeoState outperforms prior 3D world models on Waymo, supports geometrically consistent cross-view querying, and generalizes zero-shot to KITTI and nuScenes. Project page: https://hongchang-liu.github.io/GeoState-project-page/</summary>

    <title>3DCodeVerse: Exploring 3D Worlds as Code</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:56:07Z</updated>

    <summary>We introduce 3DCodeVerse, a research ecosystem that enables coding agents to create editable and verifiable 3D content at scale. 3DCodeVerse comprises large-scale, high-quality datasets of executable 3D code, a coding harness for spatial reasoning and automated verification, and practical guidance for 3D coding. First, we construct 3DCodeVerse-2M, a large-scale curated dataset of standalone 3D executable code. We build this corpus by collecting open-source data, converting specialized representations, and generating new programs with coding agents. Each program is packaged with the source files and associated assets required for execution in its declared environment, along with available descriptions and verification records. Second, we develop the 3DCodeVerse Harness, a multi-agent directed acyclic graph framework for generating and refining 3D content. It uses execution checks, spatial measurements, and visual feedback to automatically evaluate and revise generated programs without human feedback during generation. Third, we conduct systematic empirical studies of 3D coding, establishing baselines with fine-tuned open models and deriving practical guidance through component-level analyses of our harness. Extensive experiments demonstrate that fine-tuning on our dataset significantly improves the 3D coding capabilities of open-source models. Notably, our 3DCodeVerse harness achieves a 90% win rate against Claude Design (3D Object) in pairwise human evaluations, when both are utilized by Claude Opus 5.5.</summary>

    <title>Dexterity from Supervised Play</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:55:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22340v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22340v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>How can robots autonomously collect the contact-rich experience needed to learn dexterous manipulation? We present DSP: Dexterity from supervised play, a framework in which a robot learns a play policy from minutes of human play through behavior cloning, then deploys it autonomously to collect hours of interaction data to train a world model. During inference, the same play policy then guides model-predictive control (MPC) by proposing candidate action sequences for evaluation under the learned world model. To accelerate inference, we also introduce a method for distilling a closed-loop, goal-conditioned policy through self-play within the learned world model. We evaluate this framework on underactuated pushing and any-to-any in-hand pose reorientation with a multifingered hand, in simulation and real world. In real world experiment, our method outperforms hindsight behavior cloning by 69.6% in success rate and achieves comparable success to reinforcement learning with 490 times less interaction data. These results demonstrate that supervised play can autonomously collect interaction data, guide model-based planning, and enable policy learning without any task-specific demonstrations or sim-to-real transfer.</summary>

    <title>Lean Graph Search for Formal Theorem Proving</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:55:21Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22339v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22339v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Retrieving relevant lemmas is crucial for formal theorem proving, enabling provers to build machine-checkable proofs from established mathematical results. Recent retrieval systems match library declarations to a target theorem or its intermediate proof steps, but make limited use of multi-hop dependencies among declarations. These dependencies can reveal supporting lemmas that are not necessarily lexically similar to the target theorem but recur in proofs of related problems. To this end, we propose LeanGraphSearch, a graph-based retrieval method for Lean 4 that constructs a graph from Mathlib's forward dependencies and traverses it to uncover supporting lemmas through multi-hop dependency chains. Specifically, LeanGraphSearch links each declaration to the premises it depends on, uses a graph-based ranking algorithm to propagate relevance from semantically matched declarations to their dependencies, and reranks the expanded candidates against the original query. Across two mathematical retrieval benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves recall by up to 12% over the strongest baseline, LeanSearch v2, on MathlibQR and increases coverage of complete annotated proof routes on MathlibMPR, covering up to 3.7% of extra groups. More importantly, we evaluate whether these retrieval gains translate into improved end-to-end theorem proving by integrating LeanGraphSearch into an iterative proving loop guided by Lean feedback. Across three theorem proving benchmarks, LeanGraphSearch improves pass rate at {8, 16, 32} reflection turns by as much as 40% compared to vanilla prover and at most 10% compared to LeanSearch v2, showing higher accuracy-cost efficiency. These findings highlight the value of dependency graph search for theorem proving and motivate further research on structure-aware search for proof discovery.</summary>

    <title>Robust Reinforcement Learning for Dynamic Treatment Regimes under Model and Measurement Uncertainty</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:54:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22336v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22336v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We develop a robust reinforcement learning (RL) framework for learning adaptive treatment policies that generalize across patients and remain reliable under errors in the measured biomarker and shifts in the disease dynamics. By modeling the patient as a hidden context, we address generalization and robustness in a unified manner through robust contextual Markov decision processes. Applying our framework to adaptive therapy for metastatic prostate cancer in a simulator calibrated to clinical data, we obtain generalizable and robust policies that substantially outperform the existing adaptive therapy method. In particular, we attain robustness with almost no loss of performance when the biomarker is accurate and the disease evolves as anticipated, and find that the resulting policy Pareto-dominates the existing method across a diverse array of scenarios. Our findings suggest that robust RL holds great promise as a principled methodology for learning reliable adaptive treatment policies.</summary>

    <title>Evaluation Awareness Beyond English: Do LLMs Act Differently When Tested in Indic Languages?</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:53:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22333v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22333v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) can often tell when they are being tested. This ability, known as evaluation awareness, can lead models to act more cautiously during safety evaluations than in real use. Existing work has studied evaluation awareness almost entirely in English, although models serve users in many languages. Indic languages are spoken by over a billion people, yet evaluation awareness remains almost entirely unstudied in them. We test four instruction-tuned models from three families in five Indic languages alongside English. A set of cues varies whether the model is told that it is monitored and whether the monitoring is a safety test. Models refuse harmful requests more often when they are told that they are being tested. This increase appears in all four models and all six languages. In Indic languages, refusal of harmful requests rises by 14.4 percentage points on average. The test cue also brings Indic refusal of harmful requests level with English, but raises refusal of benign Indic requests from 6.9% to 11.3%. We release all 47,880 judged responses to support further work. These results suggest that safety evaluations in Indic languages may not reflect how models treat their everyday users.</summary>

    <title>KnowGPO: Knowledge-Grouped Policy Optimization for Search Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:52:33Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22331v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22331v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Deep search agents solve knowledge-intensive tasks through long-horizon, multi-turn interactions, where assigning credit to individual search decisions is fundamentally difficult. Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides only a single terminal reward shared across an entire trajectory. Recent process-supervision methods aim to assign credit at finer granularity, but they typically anchor credit to either surface-level trajectory states or model-internal signals, both of which become unreliable in deep search where observations are heterogeneous and retrieved contexts are long and noisy. We propose KnowGPO, a reinforcement learning framework that aligns trajectories by the task-relevant knowledge they have acquired rather than by their surface observations. For each query, KnowGPO decomposes the information required to derive the answer into atomic knowledge conditions, and represents the state of a trajectory at each step by the subset of conditions it has satisfied. Trajectories sharing the same knowledge state are grouped for within-group comparison, and the incremental knowledge gain between consecutive steps serves as an environment-grounded process reward. Experiments on Xbench, BrowseComp-ZH, and GAIA show KnowGPO consistently outperforms outcome-only (GRPO) and process-supervision baselines (GiGPO, IGPO) by 3.8 to 4.2 points, with our 8B model rivaling or exceeding most 32B open-source systems.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22330v1</id>
    <title>Designing Transformers for Continuous Diffusion Language Models</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:52:31Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22330v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22330v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Continuous diffusion language models (CDLMs) offer an alternative approach to parallel language generation; however, most existing studies directly use transformer architectures from either causal large language models (LLMs) or Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) for image generation, which were not optimized for CDLMs. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study on Transformer architectures for CDLMs and introduce Language Diffusion Transformer (LangDiT), combining feature and query-key normalization, wider noise conditioning, likelihood-shortcut gradient routing and calibration, and confidence-gated training self-conditioning. LangDiT significantly reduces generation perplexity in matched LangFlow comparisons, establishing a new state of the art in continuous language generation across different model formulations. Using LangFlow as a representative CDLM, LangDiT as a plug-and-play backbone leads to a new state-of-the-art model with a generation perplexity (GenPPL) of 21.72 using 1024 NFEs and 44.72 GenPPL using 128 NFEs on the unconditional generation of 1024-token sequences on the OpenWebText dataset. When adapted to Plaid-style CDLM formulations, LangDiT results in a new leading GenPPL of 11.33 using 1024 denoising NFEs, and 27.51 GenPPL using 128 denoising NFEs. These gains are achieved while retaining each model's underlying representation, training objective, and inference sampler, isolating transformer architecture as a fundamental source of improvement. Our study identifies architectural design as an important source of improvement in continuous diffusion language models.</summary>

    <title>ACEdit: Stable Multi-Turn Image Editing via Asymmetric Conditioning</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:52:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22328v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22328v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Image editing models produce impressive results for individual edits, but their quality often deteriorates over multiple editing turns. Each editing turn introduces small distribution shifts that accumulate over successive edits, creating a gap between the input distributions encountered during the editor's original training and multi-turn inference. We introduce a training scheme that makes multi-turn image editing stable under this accumulating distribution shift. A key is to force the editor to operate on its own outputs from previous editing turns during training, bringing the principle of Self-Forcing to image editing. The main challenge is that self-generated editing trajectories deviate from ground-truth trajectories, making direct supervision unreliable. We address this challenge through a distillation objective that leverages a teacher image editor to provide a reliable training signal when the model operates on its own previous outputs. We introduce an asymmetric conditioning scheme: while the student performs edits sequentially on its own outputs, the teacher remains anchored to the original clean image and receives a compound editing instruction. Experiments show substantially reduced degradation over long multi-turn sequences while maintaining editing quality and instruction adherence.</summary>

    <title>Twice Upon a Time: Complementary Representations for Time-Series Reasoning</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:52:18Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22327v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22327v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Time Series Language Models (TSLMs) enable language-based understanding and reasoning over temporal data, yet a fundamental question remains: what information should their time-series representations preserve, and what variation should they factor out? Existing TSLMs typically expose the language model to a single representation, imposing a fixed inductive bias across downstream tasks. We instead introduce complementary representations as a design principle for time-series reasoning. Our model combines two visual views: line plots preserve absolute measurements and the observed coordinate frame, while normalized delay embeddings factor out positive amplitude rescaling and offsets while exposing temporal structure. Dedicated visual encoders integrate both views into a shared language model through visual tokens and multi-level feature fusion. Evaluation-time interventions verify that the two views exhibit distinct invariance profiles, while single-view ablations show that their combination is particularly beneficial beyond basic perception, with the large gains in prediction and reasoning. Built on Qwen3-VL-8B, our dual-view model improves overall TSRBench accuracy from 44.5% with line plots alone to 53.2%, substantially exceeding the strongest evaluated dedicated TSLM baseline at 36.7%. It further achieves 89.9% accuracy on TSExam and 86.8% numerical accuracy on multivariate ChatTS alignment. Together, these results demonstrate that complementary representations provide an effective design principle for general-purpose TSLMs, enabling models to exploit temporal structure without sacrificing access to the original measurement frame.</summary>

    <title>Learning Self-Orchestration in Decentralized Agent Swarms</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:51:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22322v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22322v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The capabilities of an agent swarm depend on both its individual members and how they coordinate. Yet existing multi-agent systems often train agents within fixed orchestration structures, separating the learning of individual capabilities from the organization of collective behavior. We introduce market-based post-training (MPT), a framework for jointly learning action policies and self-orchestration in decentralized agent swarms. Agents express their willingness to participate through bids, which determine who acts and how collective outcomes provide local training credit. Learning both action and bidding behavior allows individual capabilities and patterns of participation to adapt together without a central coordinating agent. We evaluate MPT on embodied crafting, robot navigation, and deep research. Results show gains over monolithic post-training and confirm that agent participation indeed evolves with learning. With the same post-trained action policies, learned self-orchestration outperforms alternative coordination strategies. Ablations show that both action and bidding benefit from learning, and that learned bids provide more effective action-training signals. Beyond the original training objectives, trained swarms adapt faster to related tasks and achieve better performance with larger populations at inference time. Larger populations also suffer smaller performance losses under agent dropout, demonstrating that learned self-orchestration supports reuse, scaling, and robustness in decentralized agent swarms. Code and trained models are available at https://github.com/Embodied-Minds-Lab/MPT.</summary>

    <title>AVC-Reward: Event-Centric Audio-Video Consistency Evaluation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:51:56Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22321v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22321v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>As joint audio-video generation models become more capable, they can generate audio-visual scenes exhibiting three forms of complexity: multi-event composition, multi-layer audio mixture, and asymmetric cross-modal relations. However, current evaluations largely reuse metrics from earlier simple and unidirectional tasks. They typically evaluate an audio-video clip as a whole and rely on simple predefined relations, making them unsuitable for these increasingly complex scenes. We propose an event-centric evaluation framework that disentangles audio and visual events at the event level, analyzes each event independently, cross-validates relations across modalities, and aggregates the judgments into a coarse-to-fine, three-level consistency metric. The metric assesses global narrative harmony, event-level temporal synchronization, and fine-grained attribute alignment, providing a general formulation for audio-video consistency evaluation across diverse generation settings and cross-modal relations. We instantiate the metric as AVC-Reward, a trainable audio-video reward model. To evaluate the agreement between automatic judgments and human perception across generation paradigms and relation complexities, we construct AVC-Benchmark, which is primarily built from diverse positive and negative samples generated by various types of audio-video generation models. AVC-Reward achieves state-of-the-art alignment with human judgment among automatic methods, provides interpretable rationales that localize failures, and improves the audio-video consistency of a joint generation model when used as an online reinforcement-learning signal.     <title>A team of Gemini 4 Argon agents beats Minecraft</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:51:32Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22319v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22319v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We placed four Gemini 4 Argon agents in a sandboxed Minecraft survival world and gave them one goal: defeat the Ender Dragon. Each agent controlled a player via an open-source library called Mineflayer and coordinated with its teammates through in-game chat and shared memory. No one assigned roles or wrote game logic. The agents planned, wrote, and debugged every program themselves. Researchers could watch the run on a live dashboard and pause or stop it at any time, but they had no cause to intervene. Starting from a randomly generated world on Easy difficulty, the team wrote 2,783 programs and defeated the dragon in 27 hours and 14 minutes, dying 605 times along the way. To our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end autonomous completion of Minecraft by AI agents, achieved using only the standard Mineflayer library without pre-scouted seeds or other game-specific tools written by humans. Winning required the agents to keep a coherent plan across thousands of dependent steps for more than a day. Complex real-world software engineering and enterprise tasks demand the same long-horizon coding and multi-agent coordination. We describe the setup, how the run unfolded, the team's strategies (dividing the work, sharing what they learned, recovering each other's items), and the limits of the result.</summary>

    <title>Magic in quantum trajectory unravelings of noisy random quantum circuits</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:51:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22318v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22318v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The quantum-trajectory description of a noisy quantum circuit is not unique: every Kraus representation of the noise channel defines a different unraveling, i.e., a different ensemble of pure states that averages to the same density matrix. While all unravelings share the same expectation values of observables, they generally differ in the amount of quantum resources carried by the individual trajectories. Here we study non-stabilizerness, or magic, quantified by the stabilizer Rényi entropy, in quantum-trajectory unravelings of Haar-random and $T$-doped random Clifford brickwork circuits subject to local dephasing noise of strength $p$. The canonical unraveling in terms of Pauli jumps is Clifford and leaves magic untouched, so that trajectories retain the Haar-random value of non-stabilizerness. Exploring the full two-parameter family of minimal unravelings, we find that the trajectory-averaged magic can be substantially reduced by a state-independent choice of Kraus operators, and that the optimal choice is not in general the projective-measurement unraveling, but a two-outcome generalized measurement in which the Kraus operators correspond to a weak measurement of the noisy qubit. The optimal unraveling reduces the extensive magic density of the trajectories by a $p$-dependent factor without altering its linear scaling with system size. At the same time, it produces a very broad distribution of magic over trajectories, with a sizable fraction of trajectories retaining Haar-random magic. Since the cost of stabilizer-based classical simulation grows exponentially with the magic of the state, these high-magic trajectories, rather than the average, control the simulation cost. Our results delineate the potential and the limitations of unraveling optimization as a route to the classical simulation of noisy quantum dynamics with stabilizer methods.</summary>

    <title>Learning to Steer LLM Agents and Multi-Agent Systems</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:51:17Z</updated>

    <summary>Large language model (LLM)-based agents and multi-agent systems increasingly tackle complex tasks through long-horizon tool use and inter-agent collaboration. However, these systems are prone to deviating from the overall goal as execution unfolds, which wastes execution resources and leads to undesired outcomes, a failure termed goal drift. In this work, we propose a steering agent that supervises execution on the fly and steers the system back on track when drift occurs. Experiments on information-seeking search tasks show that the steering agent provides effective supervision for both single-agent and multi-agent systems, improving their performance and efficiency. The learned steering intelligence generalizes to out-of-domain tasks, transfers to unseen executors, and supports controllable intervention frequency without retraining.</summary>

    <title>Magna: simulating magic state factories as cheaply as Clifford circuits</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:51:13Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22315v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22315v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Classical simulation of magic state factories, including distillation, cultivation, and code switching, is challenging because of their substantial non-Clifford content. We introduce $\texttt{magna}$ (magic-state-factory assessment via global network algebra), a classical simulator that simulates such protocols as cheaply as Clifford circuits. $\texttt{magna}$ expresses the figures of merit of a protocol, namely the acceptance rate and the fidelity of the accepted states, as tensor networks, which it reduces globally by exploiting a structural correspondence with transversal gates on quantum codes. $\texttt{magna}$ further supports feedforward conditioned on arbitrary functions of mid-circuit measurement outcomes, including decoder outputs. We simulate Bravyi--Haah distillation with up to 100 output magic states at a cost that does not grow exponentially in the number of outputs, and achieve state-of-the-art sampling times for distance-5 magic state cultivation on both color codes and RP$^2$ surface codes. Finally, we validate nonlinear feedforward on a logical-level distillation protocol with 15 rounds of decoder-dependent feedforward. $\texttt{magna}$ aims to contribute to the key infrastructure for the large-scale evaluation and optimization of magic state factories.</summary>

    <title>Classical Capacity of Single-Mode Bosonic Gaussian Channels</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:49:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22308v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22308v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The classical capacity of a noisy optical channel is the maximum rate at which information can be transmitted reliably, given a constraint on the mean input energy. For the ubiquitous bosonic Gaussian channels, which include standard models of loss and noise in fibre and free-space optical links, determining this rate requires addressing whether entanglement between channel uses or non-Gaussian signals can outperform Gaussian encodings. More precisely, the question is whether the energy-constrained Holevo information is additive across arbitrarily many channel uses and coincides with its Gaussian counterpart. We answer these fundamental questions in the affirmative for every single-mode bosonic Gaussian channel at every input energy. Namely, we prove that independently prepared Gaussian states with Gaussian-distributed random displacements achieve the capacity, including in the low-energy regime where squeezing the signals competes with encoding information in their displacement. Our proof connects an entanglement inequality to a sharp, additive lower bound on output entropy. We then characterise communication above capacity: under a strict total photon-number cutoff, the probability of correct decoding decreases exponentially with the number of channel uses, and we derive explicit bounds on the decay exponent. When only the mean photon number is constrained, a simple energy-rescaling formula determines exactly the entire asymptotic rate--error trade-off: the capacity at mean photon number $N$ and allowed average decoding error $ε$ equals the vanishing-error capacity at mean photon number $N/(1-ε)$. Together, these results identify the ultimate limits of classical communication for some of the most fundamental models of optical communication.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22300v1</id>
    <title>Knowledge That Is Linear Before Fine-Tuning Generalizes After It</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:47:52Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22300v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22300v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Not all facts a language model can recall support further learning equally well. We distinguish active facts, which support generalization beyond their own recall, from inert facts, which can be recalled but do not support such generalization in a given task. We study this distinction by constructing new relations from existing ones. Take the relation that maps a place to its continent (Paris -> Europe) and assign each of its answers an arbitrary new label (Europe -> crab, Asia -> zebra). The new relation then maps Paris -> crab. We fine-tune the model on the new relation for a subset of subjects, without telling it the original relation or the relabeling rule, and test whether it assigns the corresponding labels to held-out subjects that share an answer in the original relation. Having learned Paris -> crab, does it answer Munich -> crab? Across eleven language models and 70 relations, how linearly readable the original relation is in pretrained representations strongly predicts this generalization. Within each model, the two correlate across relations at Pearson r = 0.87 to 0.92. This association persists when controlling, separately and jointly, for the number of fine-tuning subjects and answers, the model's accuracy on the original relation, and how often the subjects occur in pretraining text. It is also robust to re-randomizing the label assignment and fine-tuning seed, and to replacing the animal labels with labels from thirteen other semantic categories. When we map a fine-tuned model's wrong label back to the original answer it was assigned to, Munich -> zebra becomes Munich -> Asia. Answers recovered this way are more often among the linear probe's top answers for the subject than among the pretrained model's own. Whether a new relation generalizes depends less on whether its facts can be recalled than on how readily their shared structure can be read out linearly.</summary>

    <title>AI Consilium: a Benchmark of LLM Clinical Multidisciplinary Second Opinions</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:46:37Z</updated>

    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) can generate differential diagnoses for complex cases, but a useful second opinion must also be factually grounded, clinically coherent, actionable, and safe. We developed a multidimensional benchmark using 300 diagnostically resolved NEJM--MedQA cases: 110 for physician reference ratings and Judge calibration and 190 for held-out evaluation. Compared with the structured pre-consilium primary-role opinion, the complete structured synthesis had higher pooled scores across all five shared criteria, with the largest increases in problem prioritization, factual grounding, and reasoning coherence. GPT-5.6-Sol led every evaluated component and reached consensus in the fewest review rounds. These findings show that the benchmark can distinguish model capability, the contribution of multidisciplinary synthesis, criterion-specific effects of response structure, deliberation dynamics, and inference requirements within one common-case evaluation.</summary>

    <title>Private Retrieval Augmented Generation via Random Projection</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:45:51Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22297v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by querying external structured knowledge. However, it can also introduce privacy risks by leaking sensitive information from the retrieval datastore. We propose a simple method to preserve datastore privacy in RAG systems via random projection. By applying the same projection to both datastore embeddings and query embeddings, our method provably preserves semantic similarity between queries and retrieved items while substantially mitigating data extraction attacks. Across multiple RAG architectures and datasets, we show that this lightweight approach achieves superior retrieval and generation performance compared to prior methods which leverage formal differential privacy (DP) guarantees, while exhibiting comparable empirical privacy under strong attack models.     <title>Backward Compatibility in Zero-Bit Neural Audio Watermarking</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:45:27Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22296v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22296v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Neural watermarking systems are typically trained as tightly coupled embedder-detector pairs and implicitly assume static deployment. In real-world deployments, embedders and detectors are frequently updated and selectively decoupled for security and versioning purposes, which can break detection in previously embedded content and, more critically, increase false-positive rates on embedders that a given detector is intentionally not intended to recognize.
  In this paper the concept of backward compatibility in zero-bit audio watermarking is formalized. A training framework is proposed that pairs a new detector with a sequence of frozen legacy embedders (its legacy chain), using a performance-weighted sampling strategy so that the detector retains accuracy across all earlier versions. This coupling, while necessary for backward compatibility, is shown to induce an embedder-collapse effect that catastrophically degrades the true negative rate (TNR) against out-of-chain embedders. To counteract this, a Angular Diversity Loss (ADL) is introduced that explicitly forces each new embedder to occupy a distinct region of the output space. The combined approach restores near-perfect TNR with no measurable cost to detection accuracy or perceptual audio quality.</summary>

    <title>Towards Continual Learning: Mitigating Forgetting With Subspace Tuning</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:44:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22293v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) acquire new skills through fine-tuning, but it can destroy capabilities they already have: catastrophic forgetting remains a central obstacle to continual learning in LLMs. Recent works connect forgetting to how far, and along which directions, fine-tuning moves the weights. On-policy methods such as reinforcement learning and on-policy distillation avoid updating the principal singular directions of weight matrices and thus forget less. In contrast, SFT concentrates updates along these directions and is susceptible to catastrophic forgetting. In this work, we introduce Subspace Tuning (SST), which restricts each weight update to the bottom singular subspace, eliminating changes along the principal directions. SST is optimizer-agnostic and composes well with fine-tuning recipes including SFT and self-distillation. SST combines tight subspace protection, dense gradient estimation, and a simple refresh mechanism, enabling stronger learning than prior orthogonal fine-tuning methods. With these mechanisms, protecting as much as 99\% of the weight subspace substantially improves retention while preserving strong target-task performance. This behavior strengthens with model and data size and nearly eliminates forgetting in the large-model regime. SST also keeps the model close to its base distribution, inducing $2$--$4\times$ less KL drift than the baseline recipes. Overall, SST advances the learning--forgetting Pareto frontier, making it a practical default for fine-tuning pre-trained language models.</summary>

    <summary>Large language models (LLMs) are becoming prevalent in scenarios where honesty is critical. However, despite alignment training, these models still exhibit dishonest behaviour, such as outputting claims that contradict some knowledge or are not supported by what is accessible in context. CATCH trains the model towards an honest answer and away from a dishonest one while maintaining the model's capabilities. We evaluate two architectures (Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct and Qwen3-3.6-27B). We show that CATCH outperforms prompting and supervised fine-tuning in improving honesty, and it is on par with state-of-the-art honesty activation steering.     <summary>Reinforcement learning has become a common post-training technique to improve the accuracy of LLMs on verifiable tasks. However, such training can narrow the set of solutions the model can produce. Several approaches have attempted to address this behavior-sharpening effect, but they often optimize metrics that do not reflect the diversity of correct solutions. Ideally, we want a model that can produce multiple good solutions, not only a single reliable one. We propose EliteReplay, a post-training recipe that pairs GRPO with an "elite" archive built by quality-diversity search. Before training, we use the frozen base model to collect solutions that span distinct approaches; during training, GRPO is combined with a replay loss on this archive. The result is a post-trained model that improves accuracy while preserving more of the base model's solution diversity. On multiple text-to-SQL tasks, EliteReplay achieves a higher pass@128 than all baselines, producing up to 77% more distinct correct strategies than the strongest baselines. It preserves most of the base model's correct strategies, outperforming existing methods in strategy retention. This diversity translates into practical benefits on ambiguous questions, where EliteReplay covers both interpretations nearly twice as often as the strongest baseline on AmbiQT.</summary>

    <summary>Stronger language models may increasingly construct useful procedures for themselves, reducing the advantage of developer-supplied scaffolding. We investigate why this advantage persists and whether an environment-agnostic agent can be improved without environment-specific engineering. We evaluate a Codex-based agent in two nearly identical prompt variants on ARC-AGI-3, AGI Maze, and Terminal-Bench. Each variant is deployed with unchanged code, prompts, and general-purpose tools across environments, receiving environment-specific information as input. Changing only an instruction to encourage reporting difficulties and returning control for automatic continuation improves mean scores on both ARC-AGI-3 and AGI Maze, while Terminal-Bench shows small, mixed changes. Yet the general agent remains below an ARC-AGI-3-specific reference, including with GPT-5.6-sol. The reference prescribes organization and control rather than supplying new game rules or solutions. To investigate this gap, we transfer reset decisions to a scripted controller that follows a convention already given to the agent. This small change recovers part of the specialized agent's advantage. A complementary AGI Maze experiment shows that additional tutorial experience can reduce performance. Together, these findings highlight the distinction between having information and tools available and using them effectively. Supplied procedures still matter for the models tested here. The performance gains also come with higher token-based cost. The experiments do not separate better use of information and procedures from additional or differently allocated inference. We provide the EnvTraverse framework and an evaluated baseline agent for testing whether further environment-independent changes improve performance in some environments without degrading it in others.</summary>

    <summary>We study rational synthesis for stochastic multi-agent systems with unknown dynamics, where each agent is equipped with its own probabilistic temporal objective specified using Probabilistic Linear Temporal Logic on Finite Traces ($\mathsf{PLTL}_f}$). We impose solution concepts (e.g., Nash equilibrium, subgame-perfect equilibrium) as constraints on the joint strategy profile, using payoffs derived from each agent's probability of satisfying its temporal objective. In particular, we formulate per-agent rational synthesis as finding a strategy profile -- if one exists -- such that (i) the designated agent's probabilistic temporal constraint is satisfied, and (ii) the profile represents a stable solution under a chosen solution concept. We give conditional convergence guarantees for tabular Nash-Q learning, certify satisfaction with simultaneous finite-sample confidence bounds, and assess strategic stability with approximate best-response checking. Our approach operates in a stochastic \emph{Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning} (MARL) environment, where model-free learning algorithms attempt to attain extremal satisfaction probabilities for temporal objectives automatically compiled into reward automata. Our approach is empirically validated using 8 general-sum concurrent stochastic games.</summary>

    <title>Asking Smarter Questions: Targeted Active Preference Learning for Underspecified Rewards</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:41:46Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22285v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22285v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reward learning typically assumes the human's input covers everything that matters for the task. In practice, humans can only attend to so much at once, so their teaching naturally captures some features---or aspects of the task---better than others. Prior work has shown how the robot can identify which features were poorly supervised directly from its teaching data. But the current solution is to ask the human to try again, putting the burden on someone who already struggled to convey those features. We propose shifting this burden to the robot. Our key insight is that the same information that tells the robot what it doesn't know can help it ask better questions. Preference queries offer a low-effort channel for resolving this uncertainty, but only if the robot knows where to direct them and the human knows what to attend to when answering. We act on this insight in two ways: we build an informed prior that targets preference queries at the features that need resolving, and we accompany each query with an explanation that focuses the human's attention on exactly those features. In simulation, the informed prior beats the standard active preference learning baseline by up to $30.8\%$ in the low-query regime, where reducing human effort matters most. In a user study, the informed prior and explanations each significantly improve reward recovery and amplify each other.</summary>

    <title>Adding Temperature to the Adiabatic Connection: Hybrid Functionals for Static and Dynamic Correlation</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:41:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22284v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22284v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Capturing static and dynamic electron correlation simultaneously at manageable computational cost remains a key challenge in electronic structure theory. Motivated by the recurring role of effective temperature in self-consistent field methods we extend the adiabatic connection mechanism from density functional theory to include a temperature dimension. This gives rise to thermally enhanced hybrid functionals, in which static correlation is captured via fractional occupations generated by an effective "correlation temperature" within thermal Hartree-Fock, while dynamic correlation is described by established density functional approximations. The framework formally unifies information-density matrix functional theory (i-DMFT) and thermally-assisted-occupation (TAO-)DFT as special cases, clarifying their theoretical basis and the respective prescriptions for the temperature parameter. We assess the performance of several thermally enhanced hybrids for different cases where i-DMFT was previously shown to fail. Furthermore, we discuss and test different schemes for determining the correlation temperature and investigate the accuracy of different such choices for a benchmark set derived from biphenyl. The results help to clarify the achievable balance of accuracy, generality, and efficiency, establishing thermally enhanced hybrids as a systematic route toward low-cost treatment of both correlation types.</summary>

    <title>LEASH: Uncertainty-Aware Weak-to-Strong Escalation and Oversight for Computer-Use Agents</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:40:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22280v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22280v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Computer-use agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks, where running a frontier model at every step is expensive and a small open-weight model alone often fails. Weak-to-strong escalation offers a middle ground where a weak agent acts by default and hands control to a strong one only when needed. The core challenge is deciding when to escalate, which requires an uncertainty signal cheap enough to check at every step. However, even after handoff, the strong agent can still get lost, but a black-box API that the strong agent is usually served exposes no internals to monitor. To this end, we propose LEASH, a training-free framework that unleashes the strong agent only when the weak agent's latent uncertainty signals it is needed, and keeps it on a leash afterward. LEASH has three layers: (1) initial task uncertainty for early routing, (2) step-level uncertainty for runtime escalation, and, after handoff, (3) a shadow observer for continued oversight of the strong black-box agent. Here, we use latent uncertainty as a fuel for all three layers. Specifically, we compare the weak model's hidden states with those from its past successful and failed trajectories, and a state that looks more like the failures signals higher uncertainty. During weak-agent execution, our uncertainty estimator reuses activations already produced during action generation, so it needs no extra forward pass or dedicated monitor training. Experiments on OSWorld across four contemporary model backbones show that LEASH consistently improves over standalone weak agents and outperforms random escalation by 6.55--11.94 points at matched escalation rates. With Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, LEASH achieves 73.66% task success at $0.4117 per task, matching always-on Claude Opus 5 (72.90%) while reducing inference cost by 19.2%.</summary>

    <title>SynDebug: A Framework to Debug Logic Bugs in Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing Programs</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:37:29Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22275v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22275v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) introduces substantial systems-level complexity through quantum error correction (QEC), making debugging FTQC programs challenging. Existing quantum debugging approaches primarily target logical-level circuits and do not naturally support debugging within realistic FTQC execution flows. We present SynDebug, the first systems-level debugging framework for FTQC programs. SynDebug introduces lightweight assertion-based debugging primitives that operate directly within encoded FTQC infrastructures while avoiding additional logical surface area and minimizing temporal overhead. We evaluate SynDebug across multiple QEC code families, code distances, and encoded workloads, including state preparation, entanglement validation, and Shor-style programs. Our results demonstrate that SynDebug enables practical FTQC debugging with an average 1.8% additional circuit depth overhead (0% in most cases) and no measurable increase in the logical error rate, showing that systems-level debugging for large-scale FTQC applications is both feasible and practical.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22273v1</id>
    <title>Librarian Agents: Training LLMs to Curate Long-Context Workspaces that Anticipate Future Queries</title>
    <updated>2026-10-15T17:35:17Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.22273v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.22273v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Reasoning over long document contexts remains a challenge for large language models (LLMs). Standard retrieval methods are inherently reactive, bottlenecking agents with complex, cross-document reasoning at inference time, while precomputed structures like knowledge graphs often fall short because they rely on rigid heuristics. Instead, can we allow agents to perform anticipatory directed curation: learning to proactively reorganize unstructured corpora prior to inference to efficiently serve diverse future queries. We build on a key asymmetry in modern agentic harnesses (e.g., Claude Code): while LLM agents are adept at navigating existing filesystems to solve an immediate task, they are rarely trained to construct reusable workspaces for future use. To instantiate this capability, we introduce Librarian Agents, a framework in which a builder agent transforms raw documents into a hierarchical filesystem of synthetic files and reference links, which forms a workspace tailored for a downstream answering agent. We formulate workspace construction as a Markov decision process and optimize the builder policy via reinforcement learning to directly maximize downstream answering accuracy. Empirically, Librarian Agents outperforms the strongest retrieval and precomputation baselines by 33 percentage points on BrowseComp-Plus, amortizes upfront construction costs across repeated queries, and generalizes zero-shot to unseen domains on BRIGHT with a 31-point average accuracy improvement.</summary>

Central obesity and insulin resistance are also prominent features of PCOS, and in addition are important risk factors for development of hypertension, hyperlipidemia and atherosclerotic heart disease. Previous studies have suggested that cortisol is dysregulated in PCOS, primarily through increased hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis activity and enhanced cortisol secretion. Increased adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) secretion could also potentially lead to elevated adrenal androgen production in PCOS. Techniques used in previous studies have been inconsistent, however, and a link between increased HPA axis activity and the phenotypic changes in PCOS has not been clearly demonstrated. Cortisol is also produced from cortisone in peripheral adipose tissue by the enzyme 11beta-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 1 (HSD 1), suggesting another potential point of dysregulation that may contribute to central obesity and insulin resistance in PCOS. Further investigation of both central and peripheral regulation of cortisol is necessary to better understand the pathophysiology of PCOS.

Specific Aim 1: To perform a cross-sectional study of women with PCOS and normal controls matched for age and body mass index, and measure insulin sensitivity and visceral fat, as well as (a) 24-hour CPR, ACTH, free cortisol, and cortisol binding globulin (CBG), (b) adipocyte, liver, and whole body HSD 1 activity, and (c) androgen levels.

Specific Aim 2: To prospectively administer pioglitazone or metformin to women with PCOS in a placebo-controlled trial, and after one month and six months of therapy measure (a) 24-hour CPR, ACTH, free cortisol, and CBG, (b) adipocyte, liver, and whole body HSD 1 activity, and (c) insulin sensitivity, visceral fat, and androgen levels."},"conditionsModule":{"conditions":["Polycystic Ovary Syndrome"],"keywords":["Polycystic ovary syndrome","insulin","PCOS","cortisol regulation","regulation"]},"designModule":{"studyType":"INTERVENTIONAL","phases":["NA"],"designInfo":{"allocation":"RANDOMIZED","interventionModel":"PARALLEL","primaryPurpose":"BASIC_SCIENCE","maskingInfo":{"masking":"NONE"}},"enrollmentInfo":{"count":37,"type":"ACTUAL"}},"armsInterventionsModule":{"armGroups":[{"label":"A","type":"ACTIVE_COMPARATOR","description":"Pioglitazone will be given to women with PCOS. The long-term goal is to decrease cervical cancer mortality and improve women's health.","detailedDescription":"Specific Aims Eighty-seven percent of cervical cancer deaths worldwide occur in low and middle income countries (LMICs) and cervical cancer is the most common cancer in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) (1-4). The significant disparity between cervical cancer outcomes in the United States and LMICs is largely attributed to differences in screening (5). While approximately 89% of US women receive cervical cancer screening (7), less than 5% of women in LMICs have been screened (4). Barriers to screening in LMICs include challenges with infrastructure to support screening, competing health interests, lack of education, low health literacy, and poverty (2, 8-12).

In addition to the general lack of cervical cancer screening, SSA carries the highest global burden of human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection. Women account for 59% of all people living with HIV (13) and cervical cancer incidence is higher in women with HIV (14). With the advent of antiretroviral therapy (ART), women receiving HIV treatment have increased life expectancy approaching that of HIV-negative women (15). However, cervical cancer rates do not significantly decline despite ART and immune reconstitution (16), and invasive cervical cancer incidence remains high even with ART (17). The aging population of HIV-positive women will continue to face a large lifetime risk of cervical cancer (18).

Because of the burden of both cervical cancer and HIV infection in SSA, improving implementation of cervical cancer screening and treatment of pre-cancerous lesions in this region is critical. Existing methods for cervical cancer screening include cytology, human papillomavirus testing (14), and visual inspection methods (19). Pairing screening with treatment of positive screens using cryotherapy or loop electrosurgical excision procedures (LEEP) could prevent progression to cervical cancer (20), and greatly reduce morbidity and mortality in women. To address this implementation gap, simple, scalable, and sustainable interventions are imperative to improve screening and treatment of pre-cancers. The Kenyan Ministry of Health (MOH) guidelines stress the need to strengthen capacity, streamline, and standardize screening, diagnosis, and treatment of cancer (21). To achieve this, our long-term partners in the Mombasa County Department of Health (DOH) are eager to increase rates of cervical cancer screening. The investigators aim to test an implementation science methodology, Systems Analysis and Improvement Approach (SAIA), to address systems barriers to screening and provide quality improvement while relying on existing infrastructure to conduct screening. Rather than directly offering screening, this intervention aims to support systematic improvements in screening processes in facilities throughout the county. The investigators propose a collaborative research project with Mombasa County to achieve the following specific aims:

￼AIM 1:To describe the cervical cancer screening care cascade, from identification of female clients age 21-65 years old, through referral for follow-up of clients with positive or suspicious screens, in family planning (FP) clinics in Mombasa County. Following characterization of this cascade, we will conduct an analysis of correlates of failure to screen for cervical cancer in FP clients seen over a one-year period.

HYP 1: While many FP clinics are capable of providing cervical cancer screening, the majority of clients are not screened appropriately. Failure to screen for cervical cancer will be associated with both patient-level (e.g. age) and clinic-level (e.g. resources available) factors.

AIM 2: To test whether SAIA increases cervical cancer screening compared to usual procedures in a cluster randomized trial in 20 FP clinics in Mombasa County.

HYP 2: Family planning clinics randomized to SAIA will have increased rates of cervical cancer screening by modifying bottlenecks in screening processes compared to clinics randomized to usual procedures.

AIM 3: To determine the cost and budget impact of using SAIA to increase cervical cancer screening in FP clinics in Mombasa County.

Expected Outcomes and Public Health Impact As one of the leading causes of cancer mortality in African women, immediate attention to increase rates of cervical cancer screening and treatment of pre-cancers is crucial. This implementation tool holds potential for addressing gaps in cervical cancer prevention and lowering cancer morbidity and mortality. Use of the reproducible SAIA methodology could provide a template for broader rollout of cervical cancer screening throughout the country and region. Using the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR) to guide the evaluation of this intervention will provide insight about the potential generalizability of the intervention, and improve the likelihood of its successful implementation in diverse settings (22).

The proposed aims will provide valuable training in key competencies in implementation research, with measurable and objective indicators of success in skills building and career development. Therefore, the investigators want to find out whether the addition of nimorazole to the standard treatment with radiotherapy in combination with chemotherapy with cisplatin shows activity against your type of head and neck cancer and is safe.

Furthermore the investigators will investigate if a specific examination done with your tumor tissue will help to predict whether the treatment will work or not.

To find out if the activity observed with this treatment is not caused by chance alone, the investigators need to obtain data from patients who receive this treatment and from patients who receive other treatments.

The data from these two groups of patients will be compared to see which treatment is better.

Participants will be split into 2 groups. Each group will receive different treatments. The treatment each group receives is determined by chance using a computer program. If allocated to group 1, Patient will receive radiotherapy in combination with chemotherapy with cisplatin and nimorazole as a pill. This is considered the 'experimental' treatment.

Criteria:

1. Able and willing to give written informed consent and has signed the informed consent form (ICF), prior to performance of any trial activities.
2. Eligible male and female subjects aged ≥19 years.
3. Histologically or cytologically proven metastatic or locally advanced HER2 negative gastric cancer after 1st line failure.
4. ECOG performance status of 0 to 1 at trial entry.
5. Life expectancy ≥12 weeks as judged by the Investigator.
6. Adequate hematological function defined by white blood cell (WBC) count ≥3×109/L with absolute neutrophil count (ANC) ≥1.5×109/L, lymphocyte count ≥0.5×109/L, platelet count ≥100×109/L, and Hb ≥9 g/dL (in absence of blood transfusion).
7. Adequate hepatic function defined by a total bilirubin level ≤1.5×ULN, an AST level ≤1.5×ULN, and an ALT level ≤1.5×ULN. For subjects with liver involvement in their tumor, AST ≤5.0×ULN, ALT ≤5.0×ULN, and bilirubin ≤3.0 is acceptable.
8. Adequate renal function defined by an estimated creatinine clearance \>50 mL/min according to the Cockcroft-Gault formula or by measure of creatinine clearance from 24-hour urine collection.
9. Adequate coagulation function: normal international normalized ratio (INR), PT ≤1.5×ULN and activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) ≤1.5×ULN.
10. HIV patient must be stable on ART for at least 4 weeks, having documented evidence of multi-drug resistance, viral load of \<400 copies/ml and CD4+ T-cells ≤350 cells/µL.
11. HBV/HCV positive participant must be on a stable dose of antiviral therapy, having HBV viral load below the limit of quantification (HBV titer \<2000 IU/ml) and HCV RNA is not detected.
12. Has measurable or evaluable disease as determined by RECIST 1.1.

Exclusion Criteria:

1. Concurrent treatment with non-permitted drugs.
2. Prior therapy with any antibody/drug targeting T cell coregulatory proteins (immune checkpoints) such as anti-PD-1, anti-cytotoxic T lymphocyte antigen-4 (CTLA-4) antibody, or anti-4-1BB antibody, is not allowed.
3. Prior therapy with any antibody/drug targeting TGFβ or TGF receptor.
4. Anticancer treatment within 21 days before the start of trial treatment, e.g., cytoreductive therapy, radiotherapy (with the exception of palliative bone-directed radiotherapy), immune therapy, or cytokine therapy.
5. Major surgery within 28 days before the start of trial treatment (excluding prior diagnostic biopsy).
6. Systemic therapy with immunosuppressive agents within 7 days before the start of trial treatment; or use of any investigational drug within 28 days before the start of trial treatment.
7. Has persistent ≥Grade 2 toxicity that was not resolved from previous anticancer treatment, such as neuropathy (exceptions are alopecia and anemia).

* To determine the safety, DLT, and MTD of BKM120 when administered concomitantly with capecitabine in patients with metastatic breast cancer (ARM A)
* To determine the safety, DLT, and MTD of BYL719 when administered concomitantly with capecitabine in patients with metastatic breast cancer (ARM B)
* To determine the safety, DLT, and MTD of BKM120 when administered concomitantly with capecitabine and trastuzumab in patients with metastatic breast cancer (ARM C)
* To determine the safety, DLT, and MTD of BKM120 when administered concomitantly with capecitabine and lapatinib in patients with metastatic breast cancer (ARM D)

Secondary Objectives

* To characterize the safety and tolerability of BKM120 in combination with capecitabine including acute and chronic toxicities
* To characterize the safety and tolerability ofBYL719 in combination with capecitabine including acute and chronic toxicities
* To characterize the safety and tolerability of BKM120 in combination with capecitabine and trastuzumab, including acute and chronic toxicities
* To characterize the safety and tolerability of BKM120 in combination with capecitabine and lapatinib, including acute and chronic toxicities

Exploratory Objectives

* To obtain primary, archived paraffin-embedded tissues to evaluate intrinsic breast cancer subtype (i.e., HER2, luminal B, etc.) and other important predictive biomarkers (PI3K activating mutations, pAKT, p-mTOR), and explore correlations with therapeutic response to BKM120 or BYL719 in combination with capecitabine, with or without the addition of lapatinib or trastuzumab
* To evaluate the PK profile of BKM120 with concomitant capecitabine
* To examine other signaling pathway signatures
* To examine drug effect in pre- and post-treatment core biopsy specimens (optional) from appropriate patients
* To explore patient motivators for enrolling in early phase studies through patient interview

Outline:

This study is a four-arm multi-center, open-label phase I clinical trial testing the hypothesis that the addition of BKM120 to capecitabine (ARM A); the addition of BYL719 to capecitabine (ARM B); the addition of BKM120 to capecitabine plus trastuzumab (ARM C); or the addition of BKM120 to capecitabine plus lapatinib (ARM D) will be safe and tolerable as evidenced by the DLT seen. Following screening and informed consent, treatment will be initiated with one of the following:

ARM A: BKM120 PO daily for 21 days (3 weeks) plus capecitabine PO BID for 2 weeks (no capecitabine is administered during the third week).

ARM B: BYL719 PO BID for 21 days (3 weeks) plus capecitabine PO BID for 2 weeks (no capecitabine is administered during the third week of the cycle)

ARM C: BKM120 PO daily for 21 days (3 weeks) plus capecitabine PO BID for 2 weeks (no capecitabine is administered during the third week) plus trastuzumab by intravenous infusion on Day 1

ARM D: BKM120 PO daily for 21 days (3 weeks) plus capecitabine PO BID for 2 weeks (no capecitabine is administered during the third week) plus lapatinib PO daily for 21 days.

The consents are separate documents and the patient and the study team know ahead of time which Arm is open and enrolling and can therefore focus their discussion with the patient on that ARM.

Cycles in each arm will be repeated every 3 weeks (21 days). * Age ≥18 years (no upper age limit)
* confirmed pathologic diagnosis of breast cancer which is metastatic and for which capecitabine is a reasonable treatment option

  * ARMS C \& D: Histologically confirmed HER2+ breast cancer: IHC 3+ or fluorescence in situ hybridization \[FISH\] amplified; by clinical assay on either primary or metastatic tumor
* Brain metastases permitted in Arms A and B if:

  * CNS-directed treatment has been given;
  * No CNS-directed therapy for the past 3 months, including glucocorticoids; AND
  * CNS disease has been clinically and radiographically stable for at least 8 weeks
* Brain metastases permitted in Arms C and D if:

  * CNS-directed treatment has been given;

    * 4 weeks interval between whole brain radiation therapy and initiation of protocol-based therapy;
    * 2 weeks interval between stereotactic radiosurgery or gamma knife (or equivalent) and initiation of protocol-based therapy;
  * CNS disease has been clinically and radiographically stable for at least 4 weeks
  * In Arm C, if patient on glucocorticoids, must be on stable (4 weeks) dose of no more than 2 mg/day of dexamethasone or equivalent.
  * In Arms B and D, no steroids are allowed.
* Measurable or non-measurable (but evaluable) disease as defined via RECIST 1.1
* No more than 4 prior chemotherapy regimens for metastatic disease for those in the dose-escalation cohorts. Prior trastuzumab and lapatinib are allowed for the HER2+ population. Once we reach the expanded RP2D cohorts, patients enrolled must have received ≤3 prior regimens

  * Patients enrolled in ARM C may remain on trastuzumab without a washout period
  * Patients enrolled in ARM D may remain on lapatinib without a washout period
* Normal organ and marrow function as defined below:

  * Absolute neutrophil count ≥1,500/μL
  * Platelets ≥100,000/μL
